clearedSpotChecks.check: Task 4: bor's MULMOD memo at the newest tag that has it (v2.12.0-beta) and on develop. Exact reuse condition and proof that a reused reciprocal belongs to the same full 256 bit modulus.
clearedSpotChecks.note: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/0xPolygon/bor/v2.12.0-beta/core/vm/mulmod_memo.go and the develop copy; both have md5 cd596eaa6bccdd6806c03c264f4e086a. mulmod (lines 55-66) takes the memo only when z[3] != 0, and reuses mm.mu only when mm.ok and mm.mod == *z, which in Go compares the whole [4]uint64 array. On a miss it stores a value copy of *z and uint256.Reciprocal(z) before z is written. opMulmod on develop (core/vm/instructions.go:200-205) pops x and y by value and passes the stack top as z. go.mod on develop and v2.12.0-beta pins github.com/holiman/uint256 v1.3.2 with no replace for it. In uint256 v1.3.2, MulModWithReciprocal (uint256.go:688-715) and MulMod (uint256.go:720-735) differ only in where mu comes from (passed in or Reciprocal(m)), and both call reduce4(&p, m, mu) after umul with the same zero checks. I also checked that the memo is not shared between goroutines: bor's parallel processor builds a new EVM per task (core/parallel_state_processor.go:132 and :628 on develop call vm.NewEVM), and the memo is a plain field of the EVM (core/vm/evm.go:217-219). The output is therefore a pure function of (x, y, m). FullMath.sol:24, :48 and :112 compute the same words as on Ethereum. I did not rerun the Go test. No public Polygon endpoint runs the memo yet, and the medium lead for after the Salvador block covers that. The Salvador BlockAlloc code replacement at five non-PoolManager addresses (params/config.go on develop) is already in state/findings.json and is a governance action.

clearedSpotChecks.check: Task 1, erigon v3.8.1: state that outlives one instruction (frameSlots per-frame SLOAD cache keyed by ReadStamp, cacheGen, jumpDestCache).
clearedSpotChecks.note: Fetched https://raw.githubusercontent.com/erigontech/erigon/v3.8.1/execution/vm/interpreter.go and instructions.go. frameSlots and lookupSlot are at interpreter.go:95-145, the per-frame reset is at :515-516, and opSload is at instructions.go:766-786. These match the research text. opSload takes the stamp after GetState, so a warming journal entry made by the read itself is inside the stamp. I could not find the definition of ReadStamp either. execution/state/intra_block_state.go, journal.go, versionedio.go, state_object.go and access_list.go at v3.8.1 do not contain it, and eleven other guessed file names under execution/state return 404. The GitHub tree page returns 403 through the proxy. The clearance is therefore conditional, as the item itself says. If the stamp follows journal length, the only way back to a cached stamp is a revert, which restores the cached values. In that case a hook that moves slot0 between src/PoolManager.sol:196 and Pool.swap's read always changes the stamp. Even if erigon got this wrong, the effect would be an erigon-only state divergence on Ethereum, a minority client, rather than a canonical result an ordinary account could use. The existing medium lead on ReadStamp should stay open.

clearedSpotChecks.check: Task 2: long sequences (a64, a512, b, c, c2, d300, e) inside one eth_call per sequence with state overrides at each network's PoolManager address on all 21 networks.
clearedSpotChecks.note: I read out/compare.json. It has 205 rows, and the per-chain summary matches the counts in the item, including Tempo (4217) at 6 of 10 with 3 mismatches and 1 error. The listed mismatches are all Tempo: a64 steps 4-5 and d300 revert with empty data, and e reverts. One sentence in the item is wrong. It says 'In e every network returns the same ten words as Ethereum', but Tempo's e row has no words: the call reverted with WrappedError (0x90bfb865) from the hook's afterSwap (selector 0xb47b2fb1) with an empty inner reason. out/trace-4217-e.json shows an earlier stage of the same run hitting out of gas after the second CREATE2 failed with 'contract address collision'. The item does mention the collision trace. The EIP-6780 conclusion still holds for Tempo, because the collision shows the destroyed account kept its code, but the 'second swap runs the first runtime' word was not observed on Tempo. Both failures look like gas behaviour: Tempo's endpoint grants 25,000,000 gas, prices new storage higher, and a failed CREATE2 consumes the gas passed to it. Neither is a different arithmetic result. I did not rerun the eth_calls myself.
